lessons.title: Tagging the Jacket Sale
beats: Replay the $100 Ticket: You tagged a $100 jacket up 50 then down 50 as $100, writing up $50 then down $50 from the original ticket.
Spot the drawer overage: Correct price is $75, so charging your $100 ticket leaves the drawer $25 over per jacket at closing count.
Write price after rise: Pause after the 50% increase and write $150 before any decrease, so the next percent has a visible starting amount.

lessons.title: Finding Each Percent Base
beats: Find the first base: A 50% increase on $100 adds $50, because the base is the $100 ticket price before the rise.
Spot the new base: After the rise the jacket costs $150, so the 50% decrease must be taken from $150, not $100.
Compare the two halves: Half of $150 is $75, which is $25 more than half of $100, so equal percents give unequal dollars.

lessons.title: Price the Boots Clearance
beats: Record boots rise price: Boots start at $80, rise 50% to $120, and you record $120 before you touch the markdown.
Try boots markdown alone: Without hints, work out 50% off your $120 record and type that final price for the register check.
Confirm shift still applies: Half of the $120 base is larger than half of $80, so the ticket ends below the starting $80 price.

fingerprint.reasoning: Paper alone with A $100 and 'Half up, half down. Same price.' fits cancel-because-same-percent but does not show base. The follow-up that both halves are of 100 dollars and up 50 then down 50 shows both percents were applied to the original $100, not sequentially, which is sufficient to name the base error.
fingerprint.misconception: Treats both 50% changes as fractions of the original $100, so a 50% rise and 50% fall cancel
fingerprint.intervention: Have them write down the dollar price after the 50% increase before doing the decrease. Then have them compute 50% of that new price to show the base changed.
